Seven Generations of Ducati Superbikes Led to the New 2027 Panigale V4
8 photos
Photo: Ducati
When a new version of an existing motorcycle comes along, the world expects significant modifications in all departments. Yet, what Italian bike maker Ducati did with the 2027 Panigale V4 is proof that even the most minuscule of changes can have a huge impact on performance.
Building on the model that was introduced in the summer of 2024 as the 2025 model year, the Italians went all in to give the 2027MY more power, improved track times, and higher speeds. And they did that without going macro on the two-wheeler.
The main focus of the changes was the bike’s 1,103cc Desmosedici Stradale engine, which suffered targeted improvements that ended up modifying top power levels from 216 hp to 218 hp at 13,500 rpm.
That may not seem like much on paper, but in the real world it translates into 0.4 seconds gained per lap at the Vallelunga circuit during testing – and that could mean the difference between winning or losing a race. The most important changes implemented by Ducati were performed on the exhaust and lubrication systems.
On top of that, Ducati says it has improved high-RPM performance, and as a result of that, it raised the max RPM to 15,000 (up by 500 rpm) in gears from the second to the fifth. A longer final gearing was adopted, and the number of gear changes needed per lap has dropped by two.
Photo: Ducati Just like with the previous version, it is possible to take power levels even higher, by 11 hp and seven Nm of torque. That can be achieved by going for the Akrapovic exhaust system that can be installed as an option, a move that also drops the total weight of the motorcycle by 15 pounds (6.6 kg).
The frame of the Panigale V4 was not left to chance either, as, in its race to make the motorcycle faster and better, it ended up making the chassis less stiff than before and capable of taking higher mid-corner speed.
Targeting the front part of the frame, the upgrades have resulted in a 12 percent reduction in lateral stiffness. This, in turn, cascades into increased front-end grip, more precise feel during turn-in, and an improved ability to tighten the line heading into the apex.
Ducati dived into the bike’s electronics package as well, and added a new feature called the Dynamic Engine Brake. Replacing the previous Engine Brake Control, it modulates braking based on the actual load on the rear tire to provide greater stability when slowing down at lean angles.
Photo: Ducati Another technological debut on the 2027 Panigale V4 is the Race Brake Control, which is meant to increase the rear wheel’s contribution to braking power and allow for the available grip to be properly exploited.
Ducati modified a number of other components of the motorcycle, including by introducing new adjustable clip-on handlebars specifically tailored for track use and raised by ten mm to follow what’s happening in MotoGP.
Other than that, the Panigale V4 retains its curb weight of 412 pounds (187 kg), and continues to be offered with forged aluminum wheels shod in Pirelli Diablo Supercorsa V4 tires. The suspension system that ties into them, of the Ohlins variety, seems to have remained unchanged.
At the beginning of the year, the Italian bike maker launched something called the Ducati Factory Made. By trade, that’s a factory-backed customization program that gives customers the option of configuring rides to their own liking right off the factory floor.
Photo: Ducati As of now, for the first time, the S version of the new Panigale is joining the Factory Made program, giving buyers access to a choice of 11 body colors (five of which come directly from Lamborghini's Ad Personam program), two distinct liveries (Corse and Performance), and a pretty large number of accessories that can be installed right on the assembly lines.
The list includes, among others, the Pro and Pro+ versions of the Front Brake system, the STM dry clutch, and adjustable footpegs.
Ducati says the new Panigale V4, which is the culmination of a bloodline that stretches back seven generations, will be available at European dealers starting March of next year, and we expect the U.S. launch to happen shortly after that, in April 2027, with the rest of the world to follow.
There is no word on how much the motorcycle will cost yet, but the current version of the two-wheeler sells in America for prices that start at around $28,000. The bike comes from the factory floor as a single-seater, but there is the option of installing a passenger kit.
In a couple of weeks, the largest moto show in the world, the Esposizione Internazionale Ciclo Motociclo e Accessori (EICMA), opens its doors in Milan, Italy, and, even if Ducati didn’t confirm the new Panigale V4 will be there, we’ll keep an eye on things to see if we can spot it in the metal.
